Superfood Adventure Game design

What is Superfood AdventureSuperfood Adventure?

A game that teaches children what food does to them — built twice, because the first version taught by interrupting itself.

The problem of a lesson with no grade attached.

Why would anyone in the room care about nutrition?

Not the student, who is measured on maths and science. Not the teacher, who is measured on the same. India’s school system runs on marks, and a subject outside the mark scheme quietly becomes optional — while childhood obesity in urban India keeps climbing.

Could a game help you study?

All but one of sixteen students, aged 8–12, said yes.

How long does an educational game hold you?

Five to ten minutes. One session, then it gets played for the teacher rather than for itself.

Can the school computers run one?

Old machines, long loads, and crashes that take the session’s progress with them. This one turned out to matter more than the other two.

“If the teaching can be removed and the game still works, it was decoration.”

The test I hold an educational game to

How did Superfood solve this?

Make paying attention the way you win, not the price of being allowed to play.

Grading nutrition is neither realistic nor a good idea. So the brief was to replace the missing incentive rather than argue for a new one.

The food is the currency.Every food is priced in the nutrients it actually carries. There is no way to skip the nutrition, because the nutrition is the score.
Habits end you, not points.Bad points build into habits, and three bad habit cards put you out.
Printable, on purpose.Anyone with a printer makes the whole game for the price of the paper. A lost card is reprinted, not reordered.

What I did

Solo — the research, the systems, the rules, every illustration and both builds. A bachelor thesis at Anant National University, Ahmedabad, in 2023: a top-down RPG in Unity first, then a six-player board game you print at home. The second one is the design work. The first one is why it exists.

So how does a game teach without stopping to teach?

Let me walk you
through a game.

What’s on the table?

The boardOne loop of squares, with the rules printed in the middle so nobody has to hold them.
The squaresFast food, laboratory, healthy time and sports school, with time heal before start.
The decksSuperfood, fast food, food fact and bad habit cards.
The tokensYour diet, sitting on the table in front of you where everyone can see it.

What does a food cost me?

Every food in the game is priced in the nutrients it actually carries. Good points come in vitamins, calcium and fibers; bad points in sugar, fat and carbohydrates. The cost is on the front of the card, and the reason is on the back.

Which one hurts me least?

  • Burger+1 fat, +1 carbohydrate
  • Soda+3 sugar
  • Chips+2 fat

Three draws from the fast food deck

The fast-food square doesn’t let you decline. You draw three and pick the least damaging one.

Which means the only way to play well is to know which of a burger, a soda and a bag of chips hurts you least, and why. The lesson isn’t beside the move. It is the move.

How do I lose?

Bad points are not a penalty score. They build into habits, and habits are what actually end you — the argument the whole thesis is making, expressed as a rule rather than a sentence.

More than five

Bad points in one category, and you draw a bad habit card. You may then clear five of them — the damage has become something you carry.

A bad habit

Makes the rest of your game worse: one square less than you roll, an extra fat on every junk food card, or one less calcium from your superfoods.

Three habits

And you are out. The last player standing wins.

Where the game ends

What do good points buy?

You spend them at the sports school on superpowers — an extra square each turn, a bonus calcium on every superfood. Eating well is not virtue, it’s capital.

The children I interviewed had asked for exactly this: tokens you earn and spend on something you want.

Earn

Vitamins, calcium and fibers, as tokens, from every superfood.

Spend

At the sports school, on a superpower.

Where eating well pays out

Whose side is everyone on?

Every food is a character before it is a number. It starts on paper — faces, postures, a wizard and a knight that didn’t survive — and lands as flat shapes with two eyes and one expression.

Cheap to print, readable at standee size, and drawn so a child can tell the ones on their side from the ones that aren’t without reading a word.

That’s the board game.

But it only exists because the first game failed.

Version one was a top-down RPG in Unity, and everything it taught, it taught by stopping. Dr Rose is the lesson. She appears, she says the true and useful thing, and you press a key to make her go away — and the game carries on exactly as it would have if she had never spoken. That is the five-to-ten-minute problem the children described, reproduced by me, in my own build.

The laboratory — Dr Rose explains

It ran. You could walk the levels — forest, desert, ocean, a city, a laboratory — open chests, take damage and talk to Dr Rose. As the first thing I ever coded, it was the steepest part of the year.

The junk food is loot

You find a burger in a chest and nothing happens. The nutrition was a layer painted on top of the game, not anything the game ran on.

And the schools this was for couldn’t run it. A Unity build needs a machine, and the interviews had already said those machines crash.

Two ways for a game to carry a fact. The first is the one almost every educational game picks, and the one I had already built.

The fact as an interruption — what I built first

  1. Find the food
  2. Game stops, NPC speaks
  3. Dismiss the box
  4. Play resumes, unchanged

Rejected. The lesson can be skipped, and the game doesn’t notice.

The fact as the currency — what the board game does

  1. Land, draw three
  2. Read what each one costs you
  3. Choose one
  4. The choice decides the game

Taken. There is no way to skip the nutrition, because the nutrition is the score.

Where the fact sits

What it rests on

Thaler and Sunstein’s nudge, and Fogg’s behaviour model — a behaviour needs motivation, ability and a prompt at the same moment.

A game is unusually good at all three: it supplies the motivation, keeps the ability trivial, and prompts on every turn.

What the table changed

Groups played it, and three rules changed because of what they did rather than what I intended. Superpowers became recipes, costing ingredient cards from a new farm square. Every bad habit card now carries an exercise you do when you take it. And players who hoarded now discard over five cards.

Printable, on purpose

A manufactured board game inherits a supply chain — and a game handed to nine-year-olds loses a token in week one. So the deliverable is a file: about ₹1 a page, 10–20 pages, and a translation is an edit rather than a manufacturing run.

What went over

The board game is finished, playable, and has been played. The RPG is not, and I’d rather say that than dress version one as a companion piece.

What the year produced was a design argument I still hold: a lesson a player can dismiss is a lesson the game does not need. Making the nutrition into the currency was the only move that made it structural.

What I’d do differently

Nothing here measures whether anyone learned anything — no knowledge check before and after a session, no follow-up on what children ate. And the sixteen interviews were with students at urban private schools in four cities: close to the least likely group to need a game you print because the computers don’t work.

So: put one printed copy in a classroom without working computers, and run a five-question check before the session and the same five after. And keep the RPG in the process, not the deliverable — it earned its place as the reason for the pivot, not as a second product.
